title: Young winners
description: The Young winners: the candidates that become weak Condorcet winners after deleting the fewest voters (Theta-2-complete, Rothe, Spakowski and Vogel 2003). The loop generates rows lazily: A deletes the fewest voters so that no opponent found so far beats its winner, C finds an opponent that still does, and the refinement grounds that opponent's majority constraint for every winner at once (refine(k)). Compare with implicit hitting sets whose cores name the winner, and with all constraints from the start.
readme:
# Project: Young winners

## Research question

A Young score (Young 1977) is the least number of voters to delete so that no candidate beats the
winner; the winner problem is Theta-2-complete (Rothe, Spakowski and Vogel 2003). Its
constraints are one majority count per opponent, so few of them matter. Which refinement learns
them best: the whole constraint of an opponent (a rule), or a core that forces one more deletion?

## The loops

- **default**: row generation. A deletes the fewest voters so that no opponent found so far beats
  its winner; C finds an opponent that still does, and `refine(k)` grounds that opponent's
  constraint for every winner. At most m - 1 refinements.
- **cores**: implicit hitting sets with a witness check. A minimal core names the winner and a set
  of kept voters of whom one must go: one more deletion per core.
- **plain-cores**: the same with the cores as clasp returns them.
- **all-opponents**: every constraint from the start (no refinement).
- **exists-forall**: the Sigma-2 template with one-literal clauses `atmost(S)`.

## Baseline

Time of a run with all solutions on clingo-wasm (`tools/bench.mjs`, suite `loops`, limit 60 s, two runs at a time) and, in brackets, the refinements added, counting the blocks that rule out a winner. The small instances take under 0.2 s with every loop.

| instance | default | cores | plain-cores | all-opponents | exists-forall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1964: 9 drivers | 0.0 s (12) | 0.2 s (58) | 0.1 s (103) | 0.1 s (9) | 0.0 s (8) |
| 1970: 9 drivers | 0.1 s (15) | 0.1 s (33) | 0.1 s (58) | 0.1 s (9) | 0.1 s (4) |
| 1978: 20 drivers | 0.2 s (25) | 0.5 s (72) | 0.3 s (103) | 0.2 s (20) | 0.1 s (2) |
| 1993: 23 drivers | 0.1 s (24) | 0.2 s (45) | 0.1 s (45) | 0.2 s (23) | 0.1 s (2) |
| 1991: 31 drivers | 0.2 s (32) | 0.5 s (61) | 0.2 s (61) | 0.2 s (31) | 0.2 s (2) |
| Latin square: 5, 65 voters | 0.2 s (10) | > 60 s | > 60 s | 0.3 s (5) | 0.3 s (2) |

Row generation needs one refinement per opponent that matters; a core forces one more deletion, so on the Latin square (Young score 27) the core variants need dozens of rounds per winner and do not finish in a minute.

## Things to try

- Strict Young (no candidate ties with the winner) and the variant that keeps the most voters.
- Cores of a check that may delete voters itself (an OLL loop per winner).
- Which opponents does row generation find first, and does the order matter?

## How to measure

Each suite runs its variants on the instances (Campaign tab, Advanced mode); headless:
`node tools/bench.mjs young-winners --suite loops --out rows.jsonl` and `node tools/report.mjs rows.jsonl`.
The instances tagged `slow` and `bench` (the larger F1 seasons and the Latin square) are where the loops differ;
they run in the suites, never in the tests;
the small ones are for the audit (`node tools/audit.mjs young-winners --instance all --link G`) and the tests.
The suite `mallows` draws elections of 6 to 10 candidates. Every expected count was checked
against an independent encoding with clingo's own optimisation, or by brute force on the small ones.

## References

- H. P. Young. Extending Condorcet's rule. *Journal of Economic Theory* 16(2):335–353, 1977.
- J. Rothe, H. Spakowski and J. Vogel. Exact complexity of the winner problem for Young elections. *Theory of Computing Systems* 36(4):375–386, 2003.
- J. Davies and F. Bacchus. Solving MAXSAT by solving a sequence of simpler SAT instances. *CP 2011*, LNCS 6876, 225–239.
- N. Mattei and T. Walsh. PrefLib: a library for preferences. *ADT 2013*, LNCS 8176, 259–270. Data: dataset 00052 (Formula 1 seasons), https://www.preflib.org.

fragments.name: shared
fragments.text:
% The election is the instance (Instances tab). ballot(V,(A,B,...)): voter V ranks A first,
% B second, and so on; count(V,N) (optional): N voters cast this ballot, as in PrefLib's
% "N: a,b,...". Ballots of 3 to 12 candidates are read below; for more, give rank(V,P,X).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J;V,11,K) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J;V,11,K;V,12,L) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K,L)).
% rank(V,P,X): voter V puts candidate X in place P.
cand(X) :- rank(_,_,X).
#defined count/2.
votes(V,N) :- rank(V,1,_), N = #max { 1; M : count(V,M) }.
% n(X,Y,N): N voters prefer X to Y.
n(X,Y,N) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X != Y, N = #sum { W,V : rank(V,I,X), rank(V,J,Y), I < J, votes(V,W) }.
% edge(X,Y,M): a majority prefers X to Y, by a margin of M votes.
edge(X,Y,N-K) :- n(X,Y,N), n(Y,X,K), N > K.
% unit(V,K): the K-th of the voters who cast ballot V. prefers(V,X,Y): ballot V ranks X above Y.
unit(V,K) :- votes(V,N), K = 1..N.
prefers(V,X,Y) :- rank(V,I,X), rank(V,J,Y), I < J.
fragments.description: The election: pairwise counts, the voters one by one. Added to every solver.

fragments.name: winner
fragments.text:
% A candidate: one winner.
1 { top(X) : cand(X) } 1.
#show top/1.

fragments.name: deletions
fragments.text:
% ... and the voters to delete: del(V,K), the K-th voter with ballot V. Voters with the
% same ballot are interchangeable: delete the K-th only if the (K-1)-th goes too.
{ del(V,K) : unit(V,K) }.
:- del(V,K), K > 1, not del(V,K-1).
% The cost: the number of deleted voters, the Young score if no candidate beats the winner.
#minimize { 1,V,K : del(V,K) }.
#show del/2.
fragments.description: Solver A: the voters to delete, as few as possible.

fragments.name: opponents
fragments.text:
% Row generation: one constraint per opponent the check has found. cex(k,opp(D)): after the
% deletions, D beat the winner of the k-th candidate. From now on D beats no winner: of the
% voters left, at least as many prefer the winner to D as the other way round. (k is the
% number of the refinement; do not name a constant k.)
#program refine(k).
:- cex(k,opp(D)), top(X), D != X, n(X,D,A), n(D,X,B),
   #sum { 1,V,K : del(V,K), prefers(V,D,X) ; -1,V,K : del(V,K), prefers(V,X,D) } < B - A.
fragments.description: Solver A: refine(k) grounds the majority constraint of an opponent found by the check.

fragments.name: glue
fragments.text:
% The check reads the winner and the deleted voters.
glue(top(X)) :- cand(X).
glue(del(V,K)) :- unit(V,K).
fragments.description: Link G: the winner and the deleted voters.

fragments.name: glue_top
fragments.text:
% The winner on a link of its own: W.block(M) rules it out.
glue(top(X)) :- cand(X).

fragments.name: beaten
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: an opponent D that still beats the winner after the deletions.
1 { opp(D) : cand(D) } 1.
:- opp(D), top(D).
:- opp(D), top(X), n(X,D,A), n(D,X,B),
   #sum { 1,V,K : del(V,K), prefers(V,D,X) ; -1,V,K : del(V,K), prefers(V,X,D) } >= B - A.
#show opp/1.
% No relevant/1: the loop grounds D's constraint in A (refine), for every winner at once.
fragments.description: Solver C: an opponent that still beats the winner after the deletions.

fragments.name: weak
fragments.text:
% After the deletions no candidate D beats the winner X: of the voters left, at least as many
% prefer X to D as D to X (X is a weak Condorcet winner of them). Each deleted voter who
% prefers D to X takes one vote from D, each who prefers X to D one from X.
:- top(X), cand(D), D != X, n(X,D,A), n(D,X,B),
   #sum { 1,V,K : del(V,K), prefers(V,D,X) ; -1,V,K : del(V,K), prefers(V,X,D) } < B - A.
fragments.description: The majority constraints of every opponent: solver A of all-opponents, the witness check of cores, both solvers of exists-forall.

fragments.name: score
fragments.text:
% The number of deleted voters in order encoding: atmost(S) holds for S at least that number.
maxdel(U) :- U = #count { V,K : unit(V,K) }.
atmost(S) :- maxdel(U), S = 0..U, #count { V,K : del(V,K) } <= S.
fragments.description: Solver A of the variant exists-forall: the number of deletions, in order encoding.

fragments.name: fewer
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: a winner (any) for whom fewer deletions suffice than the candidate's.
:- atmost(S), #count { V,K : del(V,K) } >= S.
% It refutes every candidate that deletes more: the clause is atmost(S), with S its deletions.
relevant(atmost(S)) :- S = #count { V,K : del(V,K) }.
fragments.description: Solver C of the variant exists-forall: a winner that needs fewer deletions.

fragments.name: glue_score
fragments.text:
% The check reads the candidate's number of deletions.
maxdel(U) :- U = #count { V,K : unit(V,K) }.
glue(atmost(S)) :- maxdel(U), S = 0..U.
fragments.description: Link G of the variant exists-forall: the score.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + winner + deletions + opponents
solver C = shared + beaten
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# Row generation (lazy constraints): A deletes the fewest voters so that
# no opponent found so far beats its winner; C finds an opponent that still does, and the
# refinement grounds that opponent's majority constraint, for every winner at once. With
# m candidates there are at most m - 1 refinements. A candidate without a counterexample
# is optimal for its winner; the first one has the best Young score.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    if best != none and M.cost > best:
        A.add(W.block(M))                # its least number of deletions exceeds the best
        continue
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(opp/1))
        count opponents
    else:
        log "Young winner", M.value(top/1), "deletes", M.cost
        accept M
        best = M.cost
        A.add(W.block(M))

% Eight voters, five candidates, no Condorcet winner: the majority prefers b to e, e to d and
% d to b. The four rules of the Voting group pick four different sets of winners here.
ballot(1,(e,d,b,a,c)).  count(1,3).
ballot(2,(b,e,d,c,a)).
ballot(3,(a,d,b,e,c)).
ballot(4,(d,b,c,a,e)).
ballot(5,(a,b,e,c,d)).  count(5,2).

% The Condorcet paradox: each candidate loses to another one two votes to one, so every
% rule ties all three.
ballot(1,(a,b,c)).
ballot(2,(b,c,a)).
ballot(3,(c,a,b)).

% A Condorcet winner, b, which beats every other candidate head to head although a and c have
% more first places. All four rules pick it alone.
ballot(1,(a,b,c,d)).  count(1,2).
ballot(2,(c,b,d,a)).  count(2,2).
ballot(3,(b,d,a,c)).

% Eleven voters, five candidates. Kemeny picks e, Slater a, Dodgson c and e, Young d and e.
ballot(1,(a,c,b,d,e)).  count(1,2).
ballot(2,(e,d,a,b,c)).  count(2,2).
ballot(3,(c,a,b,d,e)).
ballot(4,(c,e,a,d,b)).  count(4,3).
ballot(5,(d,e,a,c,b)).  count(5,3).

generators.name: election-mallows
generators.description: v voters over the first m of the candidates a..j, each ranking them by a Mallows model around a, b, c, ... with dispersion phi/1000 (1000 = impartial culture).
generators.text:
% election-mallows: v voters over the candidates a, b, c, ... (the first m, at most 10); voter V
% puts candidate I in place @mallows(m, phi, I, V) of a Mallows ranking around a, b, c, ...
% (dispersion phi/1000: 0 = everyone agrees, 1000 = impartial culture).
name(1,a;2,b;3,c;4,d;5,e;6,f;7,g;8,h;9,i;10,j).
voter(1..v).
rank(V,@mallows(m,phi,I,V),X) :- voter(V), name(I,X), I <= m.
#show rank/3.

generators.name: election-latin
generators.description: A Latin square: the m cyclic shifts of the ranking a, b, c, ..., each cast by lo to hi voters. No Condorcet winner unless the counts are lopsided; large Dodgson and Young scores.
generators.text:
% election-latin: the m cyclic shifts of the ranking a, b, c, ... (m at most 10), shift S cast
% by @int(lo, hi, S) voters. Every candidate is in every place once, so the counts decide.
name(1,a;2,b;3,c;4,d;5,e;6,f;7,g;8,h;9,i;10,j).
shift(0..m-1).
rank(S+1,P,X) :- shift(S), P = 1..m, name(I,X), I = (P - 1 + S) \ m + 1.
count(S+1,@int(lo,hi,S)) :- shift(S).
#show rank/3.
#show count/2.

variants.name: cores
variants.note: Implicit hitting sets: a witness check, refined by minimal cores that name the winner and voters of whom one must go.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + winner + deletions
solver C = shared + weak
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# Implicit hitting sets with cores that name the winner: C is a witness check (no candidate
# beats the winner after the deletions). A minimal core is the winner plus a set of kept
# voters of which one must go: the clause "another winner, or delete one of these". Each core
# forces one more deletion, so a large majority against the winner takes many rounds.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    if best != none and M.cost > best:
        A.add(W.block(M))                # its least number of deletions exceeds the best
        continue
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        log "Young winner", M.value(top/1), "deletes", M.cost
        accept M
        best = M.cost
        A.add(W.block(M))
    else:
        A.add(C.core.minimal.on(G))
        count cores

variants.name: plain-cores
variants.note: The variant cores with the cores as clasp returns them (C.core).

loop.text:
solver A = shared + winner + deletions
solver C = shared + weak
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# Implicit hitting sets with cores that name the winner: C is a witness check (no candidate
# beats the winner after the deletions). A minimal core is the winner plus a set of kept
# voters of which one must go: the clause "another winner, or delete one of these". Each core
# forces one more deletion, so a large majority against the winner takes many rounds.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    if best != none and M.cost > best:
        A.add(W.block(M))                # its least number of deletions exceeds the best
        continue
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        log "Young winner", M.value(top/1), "deletes", M.cost
        accept M
        best = M.cost
        A.add(W.block(M))
    else:
        A.add(C.core.on(G))
        count cores

variants.name: all-opponents
variants.note: No refinement: every majority constraint in A from the start, one optimal solve per winner.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + winner + deletions + weak
solver C = shared + beaten
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# No refinement: A has the majority constraints of every opponent from the start, so each
# optimal model is a winner with its Young score. The check never finds an opponent.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    if best != none and M.cost > best:
        A.add(W.block(M))
        continue
    if C.solve(assume G(M)): stop "an opponent beats an optimal winner"
    log "Young winner", M.value(top/1), "deletes", M.cost
    accept M
    best = M.cost
    A.add(W.block(M))

variants.name: exists-forall
variants.note: The Sigma-2 template: a winner with its deletions against a winner with fewer; one-literal clauses atmost(S) from relevant/1.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + winner + deletions + weak + score
solver C = shared + winner + deletions + weak + fewer
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue_score
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# The Sigma-2 template on a Theta-2 problem: A proposes a winner and deletions that make it a
# weak Condorcet winner; C looks for any winner that needs fewer deletions. The clause from
# relevant/1 is one literal, atmost(S): a bound on the score, valid for every winner.
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.add(G.clause(M, X))        # from now on: at most S deletions
    else:
        log "Young winner", M.value(top/1), "deletes", M.count(del/2)
        accept M
        A.add(W.block(M))
